description: Add two signed 32-bit integers without using arithmetic operators or an arithmetic helper. Return the signed 32-bit two's-complement sum: overflow wraps modulo 2^32, exactly as ordinary Java int addition. Use bit operations to combine sum bits and carries.
constraints: Both inputs may be any signed 32-bit integer. Preserve their caller values. For example 2147483647 plus 1 returns -2147483648, not an exception or a wider positive result.

Do not use addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, remainder, increment/decrement, sum helpers or conversion to a representation that delegates addition. Bitwise operations, masks, shifts, comparisons, assignment and loops/recursion are allowed. C++ fixed-width bit reinterpretation is allowed; it performs no arithmetic.
why: XOR gives the sum bits that need no carry. AND identifies positions where both operands contain a one, and shifting those positions left produces pending carries. Repeat with the carry-free result and pending carries until no carries remain. Fixed-width masking is essential in Python, where negative integers do not automatically have 32-bit width.
correctness: For each bit position, XOR contributes the low sum bit and the shifted AND contributes its carry into the next position. Replacing the operands by those two patterns preserves their total modulo 2^32. Each pending carry moves left, so after at most 32 rounds none remains within the word. The remaining pattern is therefore the required modular sum. C#/Java/JavaScript naturally observe the fixed-width pattern; Python masks each carry and reinterprets the final sign. C++ uses unsigned shifts and a fixed-width byte copy for the signed result, avoiding undefined signed left shift or narrowing.
walkthrough: For 5 and 3, the first XOR is 6 and the pending carry is 2. Next they become 4 and 4, then 0 and 8, then 8 and 0. The returned result is 8. For -1 and 1, the carry propagates through the whole word and is discarded above bit 31, leaving zero.
time: O(w) bit-operation rounds for a w-bit word, at most 32 here; therefore bounded O(1) for this fixed-width callable.
space: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage; iterative implementations use no recursion stack.
edges: Zero, equal values, negative values and long carry chains.
Both signed endpoints and sums that wrap across either endpoint.
related: The author public test intentionally includes overflowing addition; an unbounded mathematical-sum contract would differ.
title: Add Without Plus

description: The hidden array contains every integer from 0 through n except one, in arbitrary order, where n=numbers.Size(). Find the missing integer using only individual-bit queries. The judge provides BitArray with Size() and FetchBit(index,column). Column 0 is the least significant bit; column 31 is the most significant bit of the nonnegative 32-bit value. Each FetchBit returns exactly 0 or 1.
constraints: The hidden array has n in 0..10000 entries, all distinct, and is exactly {0,..,n} with one member omitted. You may read Size() and call FetchBit at index 0..n-1 and column 0..31. Empty input therefore has missing value 0.

The numeric array shown in examples/test fixtures is only a wire representation. Your callable receives BitArray, never an integer array. No full-integer accessor, mutable element, enumeration or private-state inspection is permitted. Use at most 4*n+32 FetchBit calls. Arithmetic on array indices, counts and the constructed missing answer is allowed; reconstructing every hidden integer is outside the bit-only linear-query task.
The provided hidden values and order are readonly. Local lists of original indices may be allocated and partitioned. Do not redeclare or replace the bank-provided BitArray API.
why: At the least significant bit, a complete consecutive range has as many zeros as ones or one extra zero. Removing a zero leaves zero-count no larger than one-count; removing a one leaves more zeros. This identifies the missing low bit without reconstructing any number. Retain only indices with that bit, discard the known low bit conceptually, and repeat. Each retained set shrinks by roughly half.
correctness: At each stage the candidate values share the already determined low-bit prefix. Shifting away that prefix gives a consecutive range starting at zero with exactly the shifted missing value absent. Its even positions are either equal in count to its odd positions or one greater before removal. Therefore observed zeroCount<=oneCount identifies a missing zero bit, and the opposite inequality identifies a missing one bit. Keeping the selected partition preserves the consecutive-range-with-one-missing invariant for the next higher bit. When no candidates remain, the shifted complete range is {0}, so all remaining missing bits are zero. Accumulating the selected bits returns exactly the omitted integer. The geometric partition sizes give linear total bit queries, within the stated budget.
walkthrough: For hidden [0,1,3,4], n=4 and 2 is missing. At column 0, indices for values 0 and 4 have zero bits, while 1 and 3 have one bits. A tie selects missing bit 0 and keeps [0,4]. At column 1 both retained values have zero, so zeroCount>oneCount selects bit 1; the selected one partition is empty. Higher bits are zero, yielding binary 10 = 2.
time: O(n) individual-bit queries and index-partition work across geometrically shrinking candidate sets; at most 32 bit positions in the fixed-width model.
space: O(n) auxiliary original-index lists; hidden integers are never reconstructed or copied into local numeric values.
edges: Empty input, missing zero and missing n.
Shuffled values, boundaries around powers of two and n=10000.
Single-bit API index/column limits and the linear query budget.
related: The public exercise permits querying one bit of a hidden integer at a time. A BitArray wrapper retains that restriction while specifying a conventional least-significant-first column numbering explicitly, instead of exposing the fixture integers as ordinary callable arguments.
title: Missing Number

description: Find the longest contiguous substring containing equally many ASCII letters and decimal digits. Return its inclusive zero-based endpoints [start,end]. If several longest substrings qualify, return the one with the smallest start. Return [-1,-1] when no nonempty balanced substring exists.
constraints: text is nonnull, has length 0..10000, and contains only a..z, A..Z and 0..9. Each letter or digit counts as one character; letter case and digit value do not change its category. Preserve the input.

Return original-text indices, not a reordered selection or a count. Empty text and an all-letter/all-digit text return [-1,-1]. Punctuation and Unicode category classification are outside this shared ASCII domain.
why: Give each letter weight +1 and each digit weight -1. An interval has equal category counts exactly when its endpoint prefix balances agree. For each balance, keep its earliest prefix position; using a later occurrence could only shorten a future interval. A dense offset array suffices because every balance is between -n and n.
correctness: The difference of two prefix balances is the letter count minus digit count in the enclosed substring, so equality is equivalent to balance. At each end position, pairing with the earliest prior equal balance gives the longest balanced substring ending there. Every possible end is examined, so the longest of these candidates is globally optimal. End positions increase; keeping the first equal-length optimum also keeps the smallest start. Initial balance zero at prefix index -1 admits intervals starting at zero. No repeated balance means no qualifying nonempty interval.
walkthrough: For A1B2C the successive balances after each character are 1,0,1,0,1. Balance zero at index 3 matches the initial zero at -1, giving [0,3] (A1B2), length four. Balance one at index 4 gives [1,4], also length four; the earlier start wins.
time: O(n) time to scan characters and initialize the 2n+1 balance slots.
space: O(n) auxiliary first-occurrence slots, plus two returned indices.
edges: Empty input and a single category.
An optimum starting at zero, mixed letter cases, equal-length tied windows.
related: Original coordinates replace the public returned character slice; the balanced contiguous-subarray task is unchanged.
title: Letters and Numbers

python.solutionCode:
def LongestLettersDigits(text: str) -> list[int]:
    n = len(text)
    first = [-2] * (2 * n + 1)
    first[n] = -1
    balance = best = 0
    start = end = -1
    for index, char in enumerate(text):
        balance += -1 if "0" <= char <= "9" else 1
        slot = balance + n
        if first[slot] == -2:
            first[slot] = index
        elif index - first[slot] > best:
            best = index - first[slot]
            start, end = first[slot] + 1, index
    return [start, end]

description: Count all occurrences of the decimal digit 2 in the ordinary decimal representations of integers from 0 through n, inclusive. Count occurrences rather than the number of integers containing a 2: the integer 22 contributes two occurrences. Do not count leading zeros.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2147483647. Return the exact signed 32-bit count and preserve inputs. At the largest admitted n the count is 2071027783, so the return type is sufficient.
Do not construct every number in a huge range. Use integer decimal-place counting; intermediate place/block values may exceed signed 32-bit range even though the result fits.
why: At one decimal place of weight p, the digit pattern repeats every 10p numbers. Every complete block contributes p twos in that place. The final partial block contributes zero, a partial run, or a full p depending on whether the current digit is below, equal to, or above two. Add the independent counts for all places.
correctness: Write n as high*(10p)+digit*p+low with 0<=low<p. The high complete blocks contribute high*p. If digit<2, the final block has not reached its run of twos. If digit=2, that run includes low+1 numbers; if digit>2, it includes all p. Thus the formula counts precisely all occurrences at that position among 0..n. Summing over positions counts every occurrence once, including both positions in 22. Higher leading positions contribute nothing. Wide intermediates prevent overflow of 10p at the billions place.
walkthrough: Through 25, the ones place contributes 3 occurrences, in 2,12,22. The tens place contributes 6, in 20..25. The total is 9; 22 intentionally contributes to both place counts. Through 1 the answer is zero.
time: O(log_10(n+1)) decimal places; zero takes constant time.
space: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage.
edges: Zero, 2, 12, 22, and boundaries around powers of ten.
Current digit below/equal/above two; the largest signed input needs wide place intermediates.
related: Counting numbers containing a 2 is a different task; the public source counts each digit occurrence.
title: Count of 2s

python.solutionCode:
def CountDigitTwos(n: int) -> int:
    total = 0
    place = 1
    while place <= n:
        high = n // (place * 10)
        digit = (n // place) % 10
        low = n % place
        total += high * place
        if digit == 2:
            total += low + 1
        elif digit > 2:
            total += place
        place *= 10
    return total

description: Aggregate baby-name counts across synonymous spellings. Synonym pairs are undirected and transitive. Return one [representativeNameIndex,totalFrequency] row for each equivalence group, including isolated names and zero-frequency groups. The representative may be ANY original name in its group, and result rows may be in any order.
constraints: names has 0..200 distinct nonnull ASCII-letter names, each length 1..20; names are case-sensitive unless linked explicitly. frequencies has the same length with values 0..1000000, so all totals fit signed 32-bit integers. A returned name index refers to this original names array.

synonyms contains 0..10000 rows [firstNameIndex,secondNameIndex] with valid indices. Duplicate pairs, reverse duplicates and self-pairs are allowed and do not add frequency. Include an uncounted spelling in names with frequency 0 if it is needed as a synonym-chain bridge.
Every original name belongs to exactly one output group, represented once. Sum each name's given frequency once, not once per edge. Preserve all arrays, synonym row objects, values and order.
why: Synonymous names are connected components of an undirected graph. Build adjacency from the given pairs, visit each name once, and sum its frequency into that component. Mark names when adding them to the work queue so repeated/cyclic synonym declarations cannot double-count a name.
correctness: A graph path is exactly a chain of synonym declarations, so connected components coincide with the required equivalence groups. Starting at an unvisited name, traversal reaches every and only name in its component. Marking on discovery makes each name enter once, so adding its frequency once yields the exact component total despite duplicate/self edges. Later starts skip visited components, producing one row per group. The starting name is an original member and therefore a valid representative; no lexical or insertion-order representative is required.
walkthrough: For names=[John,Jon,Johnny,Chris], frequencies=[10,3,0,4] and pairs [[0,1],[1,2]], the first three spellings form one group totaling 13, including the zero-count bridge Johnny. Chris remains a separate group with 4. [[0,13],[3,4]] and [[2,13],[3,4]] are both valid results.
time: O(n+e) traversal time for n names and e listed synonym pairs, using direct index adjacency; duplicate pair contributions are still visited only as listed edges.
space: O(n+e) adjacency, visited/work queue and returned group rows.
edges: No names, isolated names and all-zero frequencies.
Transitive synonym chains, zero-frequency bridge spellings, duplicate/reverse/self pairs.
Any original representative and arbitrary group-row order are accepted.
related: Original name indices replace map key strings without losing spelling identity. The author component-frequency task permits an arbitrary representative; this grader preserves that freedom rather than demanding one canonical name.

description: Arrange the largest possible number of people into a tower so each person above another is strictly shorter AND strictly lighter. Each input row is [height,weight]. Return original zero-based row indices in top-to-bottom order, so both height and weight strictly increase along the returned sequence. Any maximum-length tower is accepted.
constraints: people is a nonnull array of 0..200 nonnull two-integer rows. Heights and weights are in 1..1000000. Equal heights, equal weights and identical rows for different people are allowed, but equality in either dimension prevents stacking that pair.
Use each original person at most once and preserve the input outer/row objects, values and order. Return original row indices, not indices in a privately sorted copy. Empty input returns [].
why: Sort original indices by height, then use dynamic programming over possible final people. A shorter/lighter predecessor can extend a valid tower; retaining a predecessor index reconstructs an actual maximum tower rather than only its length. Checking BOTH strict comparisons keeps equal dimensions from forming invalid links.
correctness: Every predecessor of a person in a valid top-to-bottom tower has smaller height and therefore occurs earlier in the private sorted order. For each person, the recurrence takes one plus the largest valid predecessor tower length, or one if none exists. Induction over that order proves each recorded length is optimal among towers ending there. The global best endpoint consequently has maximum possible length. Following its recorded predecessor links reconstructs only strict height/weight links, and reversing them yields top-to-bottom original indices. Private index sorting leaves caller rows unchanged.
walkthrough: For people=[[65,100],[70,150],[56,90]], the sorted index order is [2,0,1]. Each person can follow the previous one, so return [2,0,1]. For [[60,100],[60,90]], only one person can be used despite the different weights, because heights must also increase strictly.
time: O(n^2) dynamic-programming comparisons after O(n log(n+1)) private index sorting.
space: O(n) index, length, predecessor and returned-index storage.
edges: Empty/single person, duplicate rows and ties in either dimension.
A best tower using neither original input order nor every person; arbitrary maximum-tower ties.
related: Original row IDs replace the public HtWt wrapper references without losing person identity; the grader accepts every maximum tower, not one incidental tie choice.

languageWhy.csharp: C# sorts an int[] of original indices and compares dimensions with CompareTo, so the supplied person rows never move. The predecessor walk collects those original indices before reversing them; returning sorted-array positions would identify different people.
languageWhy.java: Java uses an Integer[] index array because Arrays.sort with a custom row comparator cannot directly sort primitive int indices. It reconstructs backward into an int[] of exactly the recorded best length, retaining original person IDs without another reverse-copy step.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ sorts only a private vector of original indices while people remains a const reference. Predecessors refer to positions in that private order; reconstruction explicitly maps each position back through order before returning the IDs.
languageWhy.python: Python key sorting caches each height/weight/index tuple once. DP predecessors index this private order, so reconstruction appends order[position], not position itself. Copying rows or sorting people in place would break the caller identity/order contract.
languageWhy.javascript: JavaScript supplies numeric height/weight/index comparisons rather than default lexical array sorting. All dimension differences are exact in the admitted range. The saved predecessor positions are mapped back to original indices before reversing the local result.

title: Circus Tower

description: Return the zero-indexed kth number in the increasing sequence of positive integers whose only prime factors are 3,5 and 7. Include 1 as the empty product at index zero. Each distinct value appears once even if several multiplication histories produce it.
constraints: 0 <= k <= 500. The sequence starts 1,3,5,7,9,15,21,25,27. Preserve inputs. The index is zero-based, matching the author public implementation, not a one-based rank.
At index 500 the result is 284765625. Even seven times that value fits signed 32-bit range, so every candidate computed under this bound is safe. Do not include factors 2 or any other prime.
why: Merge the increasing sequences obtained by multiplying already generated values by 3,5 and 7. One pointer per factor identifies its smallest candidate not yet emitted. Pick the minimum candidate, then advance EVERY pointer that produced it so a value such as 15 is not emitted twice.
correctness: Initially the generated list contains only 1. Every other permitted number is a smaller permitted number times at least one of 3,5,7. Each pointer skips exactly candidates already emitted; hence the minimum of their next candidates is the smallest permitted value still missing. Appending it maintains increasing complete order. Advancing all equal producers removes duplicate histories without removing a distinct value. By induction list[k] is exactly the requested zero-indexed value.
walkthrough: After 1, candidates 3,5,7 give 3, then 5, then 7, then 9. The value 15 is produced both as 3*5 and 5*3. Both responsible pointers advance when 15 is appended, so the next output is 21 rather than another 15. Therefore index 5 returns 15.
time: O(k+1) time: one constant-size minimum and three possible pointer advances per generated value.
space: O(k+1) stored sequence values and three pointers.
edges: Index zero, first few values, and duplicate-producing products such as 15 and 105.
Largest admitted index with no signed multiplication overflow.
related: An ugly-number sequence allowing prime factor 2 is not an exact replacement.
title: Kth Multiple

description: Find a value occurring strictly more than half the time in values. Return [value] if such a majority exists, otherwise return an empty integer collection. A value appearing exactly half the time is not a majority. Preserve the input.
constraints: values contains 0..10000 signed 32-bit integers, including -1 and both signed endpoints. The optional result is a concrete zero- or one-element integer array/list/vector.
The collection wrapper distinguishes no majority from a legitimate majority whose value is -1. Empty input has no majority. At most one value can occur strictly more than half the time.
why: Cancel pairs of different values: a strict majority cannot be eliminated by these cancellations, because each canceled majority occurrence removes a nonmajority occurrence too. Keep a candidate and an unmatched balance instead of storing all counts. Cancellation produces only a candidate, so a second pass must verify that it actually exceeds half the original length.
correctness: When the balance reaches zero, all processed values can be partitioned into unlike canceled pairs. A positive balance represents that many uncanceled copies of the candidate. Removing unlike pairs preserves the identity of any strict majority, so if one exists it is the final candidate. The second pass counts that candidate in the original array and returns it only if its count exceeds floor(n/2), proving both soundness and completeness. With no majority, including empty input, verification returns the empty collection.
walkthrough: For [2,1,2,3,2], cancellation leaves candidate 2. Verification finds three copies among five values, so return [2]. For [1,2,3], a candidate still survives the first pass, but its single occurrence is not a majority, so return [].
time: O(n) time for cancellation and verification scans.
space: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage plus a result containing at most one integer.
edges: Empty input, a singleton, exactly-half frequency, no majority.
A genuine -1 majority, signed endpoints, and a candidate requiring second-pass rejection.
related: The public -1 absence sentinel is ambiguous for signed inputs; the explicit optional-value wrapper preserves the task without restricting its values.
title: Majority Element

description: Return the smallest absolute difference between an occurrence index of first and an occurrence index of second in the tokenized text words. Count index steps, not just intervening words. Return -1 if either requested word is absent.
constraints: words contains 0..10000 nonnull lowercase ASCII words, each 1..20 letters. first and second are distinct nonempty lowercase ASCII words of length at most 20. Matching is case-sensitive and requires a complete token.

Preserve words and its order. Positions are zero-based. Adjacent requested words have distance 1, and two equal query words are outside this callable's domain. This is the single-query task; no persistent index is supplied.
why: Remember the most recent position of each requested word. When one appears, its closest partner among all earlier opposite-word occurrences is the latest such occurrence. Updating the best distance at those encounters finds every possible closest cross-word boundary without storing all positions.
correctness: For any occurrence at index i, every earlier opposite-word index j has distance i-j. This distance is smallest for the largest such j, which is exactly the remembered last position. Every pair has a later endpoint; when that endpoint is scanned, the algorithm considers a pair at least as close. Taking the least of these candidate distances therefore finds the global minimum. Only actual occurrences update remembered positions, so every candidate is valid. If either word never occurs, no candidate exists and the explicit -1 result is correct.
walkthrough: For words=[red,x,blue,red,y,blue], first=red and second=blue, the encounter at index 2 yields distance 2 from red at 0. The red at index 3 is only 1 away from blue at 2, improving the best to 1. The final blue is 2 away from red at 3, so return 1, not zero intervening words.
time: O(n*L) worst-case character comparison work for n tokens and maximum word length L; O(n) token comparisons.
space: O(1) auxiliary index/count storage.
edges: Empty text, one or both words absent.
Adjacent targets, repeated runs and the closest pair appearing late.
related: The author public single-query scan returns a location pair. This callable exposes its minimum index distance and explicitly defines absence and distinct-query behavior.

description: Split a spaceless text into nonempty tokens so the total number of characters in unrecognized tokens is as small as possible. A token is recognized exactly when it appears in dictionary. Return the actual token sequence, whose concatenation must equal text. Any minimum-cost tokenization is accepted; no characters may be deleted, changed or reordered.
constraints: text is a nonnull string of 0..200 lowercase ASCII letters. dictionary is a nonnull array of 0..200 nonempty lowercase ASCII words of length at most 20. Duplicate entries are vocabulary duplicates, not consumable supplies. A known word may be used repeatedly.

An unrecognized token costs its full character length. Unknown text may be grouped or split into individual-character tokens at the same cost. Empty text returns []; empty tokens are invalid. Preserve dictionary order/entries and text.
why: A prefix either ends with one unrecognized character, costing one extra, or with a recognized dictionary word, costing nothing beyond the best preceding prefix. Considering every dictionary-length suffix handles overlapping word choices that greedy splitting can miss. Save the chosen preceding position to reconstruct tokens as well as the minimum cost.
correctness: Every produced tokenization ends in either a recognized word or an unrecognized segment. The latter can be split into single unknown characters without changing its cost, so the recurrence considering one unknown character is sufficient. Removing the final recognized word or unknown character leaves a strictly shorter prefix with optimal cost by induction. Taking the minimum over these possibilities therefore gives the global minimum. Saved predecessor positions strictly decrease during reconstruction and concatenate to the complete original text, proving both valid coverage and minimum cost.
walkthrough: For text=abcd and dictionary=[ab,abc,cd], choosing the longest first word abc leaves unknown d with cost 1. Prefix DP instead finds ab+cd with cost 0 and returns [ab,cd]. For text=xyz with no dictionary, [x,y,z] and [xyz] both have minimum cost 3 and are accepted.
time: Expected O(D+N*L^2) character work for D dictionary characters, text length N and maximum dictionary word length L: at most L suffix checks per prefix, each copying/hashing up to L characters. Hash collisions can worsen lookup.
space: O(D+N) dictionary and DP/predecessor/output storage, plus O(L) temporary substring characters.
edges: Empty text or dictionary, all-known and all-unknown text.
Overlapping words where greedy longest-prefix choice fails; repeated vocabulary use and multiple optimal tokenizations.
related: The public ReSpace task returns an actual parsing, not only its invalid-character count. Returned tokens make that reconstruction executable and allow every optimum tie.

description: Return the k smallest input values in nondecreasing order, preserving duplicate occurrences. The output has exactly k elements. Do not change the input array or its order.
constraints: values contains 0..10000 signed 32-bit integers, and 0 <= k <= values.length. For k=0 return an empty integer collection. Signed endpoints and repeated equal values are admitted.

Use an auxiliary max heap of at most k values rather than sorting or partitioning the input. Sorting the retained k result values is allowed. The ascending output order and the k=0 result are explicit bank conventions.
why: The largest retained value is the only one that a new smaller candidate needs to displace. A max heap exposes it immediately while keeping just k values. Values at least as large as the root cannot improve the retained multiset. Extracting largest-first in reverse positions, or sorting the final heap values, produces the required ascending output.
correctness: After the first k values, the heap contains exactly their k-smallest multiset. Inductively, a new value no smaller than the root leaves that multiset optimal; a smaller value replaces one largest retained occurrence, yielding precisely the k smallest values of the extended prefix. Equal values are ordinary separate occurrences and are neither deduplicated nor overcounted. At the end the retained multiset is the required answer, and output ordering changes only its order. The zero-k branch returns before accessing a heap root.
walkthrough: For [5,1,5,-2,3] and k=3, the initial heap retains [5,1,5]. Reading -2 displaces one 5; reading 3 displaces the remaining 5. The retained values are -2,1,3, returned in that order. For k=4, one 5 must remain: duplicates are not a set.
time: O(n*log(k+1) + k*log(k+1)) time including heap updates and ordered output; k=0 takes O(1).
space: O(k) heap/result storage and no input-sized copy when k is small.
edges: k=0, k equal to input size, empty input.
Repeated boundary values, negative values, and signed extremes without comparator-subtraction overflow.
related: C#/Java use reversed safe comparers, Python negates arbitrary-precision keys, C++ uses standard heap algorithms and JavaScript implements a local max heap; the explanation must match these concrete bindings.

languageWhy.csharp: C# PriorityQueue normally removes the lowest priority. A reversed Comparer makes the largest retained value leave first; CompareTo avoids overflowing a subtraction at signed endpoints. Dequeue into output positions from right to left to obtain ascending order.
languageWhy.java: Java PriorityQueue is normally a min heap. Comparator.reverseOrder makes its root the largest retained value and avoids a subtraction-based comparator that could overflow. Removing roots into the result from its last index backward gives ascending order.
languageWhy.python: Python heapq is a min heap, so store negated values: its smallest key represents the largest retained original value. Python can negate the signed minimum exactly. heapreplace exchanges one root efficiently; unnegating and sorting the retained values produces ascending output.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ make_heap/pop_heap/push_heap use a max heap with the default ordering. pop_heap moves its largest item to the back, where it is replaced before push_heap restores the heap. sort_heap finally orders the retained vector ascending. The input is read through a const reference.
languageWhy.javascript: JavaScript has no built-in priority queue here. The local down function compares both children, swaps with the larger one, and continues until max-heap order is restored. Build from internal nodes backward; after replacing the root, only that downward path can violate order. A numeric final sort orders the retained values.

description: Return the longest dictionary word that can be formed by concatenating at least two nonempty words from the same dictionary. A dictionary word may be reused any number of times as a component; this is vocabulary membership, not consuming input occurrences. If several longest words qualify, return the lexicographically smallest. Return an empty string if none qualifies.
constraints: words is a nonnull array of 0..200 nonnull strings, each 1..40 lowercase ASCII letters. Duplicate dictionary entries do not create new spellings or permit a one-component answer.

Preserve the input array and its order. Components concatenate without spaces or gaps and must spell the entire candidate. The candidate itself as one component is insufficient; at least two components are required. Lexicographic ties use ASCII letter order.
why: For each candidate, use prefix dynamic programming to record how many dictionary components can spell each reachable prefix. A valid final prefix needs at least two components, so the candidate's own dictionary membership cannot falsely qualify it. A set permits component membership checks; comparing successful candidates by length and then lexicographic order resolves the output unambiguously.
correctness: Let dp[i] be the largest number of components spelling the first i characters, or -1 when unreachable, with dp[0]=0. Every transition appends a nonempty dictionary substring to a reachable prefix, so it creates a valid decomposition. Conversely, removing the last component of any valid decomposition leaves a shorter reachable prefix; induction ensures the transition for that last component is considered. Thus dp[length]>=2 holds exactly for candidates with the required decomposition. Keeping the longest successful word and the smallest lexicographic word on a length tie produces the specified global choice. Repeated component use is allowed because membership is not consumed.
walkthrough: For [cat,dog,catdog,dogcat,catcatdog], catdog and dogcat each have two components. catcatdog has three: cat+cat+dog, so its length 9 beats their length 6 and it is returned. For [cat,dog,catdog,dogcat], the equal-length tie selects catdog. A dictionary containing only cat has no qualifying word.
time: Expected O(W*L^3) character work for W candidate entries of maximum length L: O(L^2) substrings per candidate, each costing up to O(L) copying/hashing. Hash collisions can worsen membership costs.
space: O(D*L) dictionary storage plus O(L) DP and substring workspace per candidate, for D distinct words; the input is not sorted or mutated.
edges: No composed word, repeated dictionary entries and a word that equals only itself.
Repeated component reuse, multiple decompositions and equal-length lexical ties.
related: The author task permits recursive reuse of dictionary components. The bank specifies an explicit lexical tie convention and uses independently authored prefix DP rather than its recursive implementation.
title: Longest Word

description: Choose appointments from their given sequence to maximize total massage minutes, with the restriction that no two adjacent appointments may both be accepted. Return the maximum total minutes. The empty choice is allowed; do not reorder appointments or split an appointment.
constraints: appointments contains 0..1000 nonnegative integer durations in 0..1000000 minutes. All totals fit signed 32-bit range. Preserve the original array and ordering.
Adjacency refers to neighboring input positions. Accepting index i forbids i-1 and i+1, regardless of their durations. An empty input returns zero.
why: For each prefix, an optimal choice either skips its final appointment or accepts it and therefore skips its neighbor. Only the best totals for the preceding one and two prefixes are needed. Rolling those two totals gives the full optimum without storing a table or enumerating all subsets.
correctness: Let B(i) be the best total using the first i appointments, with B(0)=0. If appointment i-1 is skipped, the optimum is B(i-1). If accepted, the remaining choices are exactly a valid optimum for the first i-2 appointments, giving duration[i-1]+B(i-2). These cases are exhaustive, and their maximum is B(i). The two rolling variables hold those earlier prefix optima before each step; updating after computing the maximum maintains the invariant and returns the full-sequence optimum.
walkthrough: For [30,15,60,75,45,15,15,45], prefix optima are 30,30,90,105,135,135,150,180. One optimal choice takes indices 0,2,4,7, totaling 30+60+45+45=180. Choosing the larger appointment from each adjacent pair independently would not enforce constraints across pair boundaries.
time: O(n) time in one prefix scan.
space: O(1) auxiliary storage for two preceding optima and a temporary update.
edges: Empty input, zero durations, one appointment.
Two adjacent large appointments; a best choice mixing early and late positions.
related: This is sequence adjacency optimization, not arbitrary time-interval scheduling.
title: The Masseuse

python.solutionCode:
def MaximumMassageMinutes(appointments: list[int]) -> int:
    one_back = two_back = 0
    for duration in appointments:
        current = max(one_back, duration + two_back)
        two_back = one_back
        one_back = current
    return one_back

description: For every pattern, return all zero-based positions where it starts in text. Include overlapping occurrences. Return one integer row per pattern, in original pattern order; positions within each row increase. A missing pattern has an empty row.
constraints: text has 0..1000 lowercase ASCII letters. patterns is a nonnull array of 0..100 nonnull strings, each 0..20 lowercase ASCII letters. Preserve the array and strings; duplicate queries receive separate identical result rows.

A pattern must match its entire text window. The empty pattern occurs at all boundaries 0..text.length inclusive, including boundary 0 in empty text. A nonempty pattern longer than text has no occurrence.
why: The direct baseline tests each legal start position independently for each query. Bounding starts by text.length-pattern.length prevents overreads, while advancing by one retains overlaps. Returning rows rather than a map preserves the order and multiplicity of the supplied query list.
correctness: A legal occurrence of a pattern of length m must start at one of the positions 0 through n-m, and the loop examines each exactly once. Character-by-character equality (or equivalent exact substring comparison) accepts precisely the windows spelling that pattern, so no occurrence is missed or invented. Increasing start order yields increasing output positions and includes overlaps. For m=0, each of the n+1 legal windows is empty, giving the stated boundary convention. An outer loop over patterns preserves every query position, including duplicates.
walkthrough: For text=ababa and patterns=[aba,ba,z,""], aba starts at [0,2], ba at [1,3], and z has no match. The empty pattern row is [0,1,2,3,4,5]. The two aba occurrences overlap at index 2; moving by pattern length would miss one.
time: O(P+sum(max(0,n-m+1)*(m+1))) worst-case time over P patterns of lengths m and text length n; this is the direct baseline, not a trie-optimized search.
space: O(K+P+L) for K returned positions, P result rows and at most L temporary substring characters; constant comparison indices beyond the output in versions using direct character comparison.
edges: Empty text/pattern, missing pattern and a pattern longer than text.
Overlaps, repeated queries and matches at the final legal start.
related: The author public direct baseline establishes inclusive start enumeration, including empty patterns. Per-query rows replace its map without silently losing repeated queries.

description: Return inclusive zero-based endpoints [start,end] of the shortest contiguous subarray of big containing every value from small at least once. The values of small may appear in any order inside the subarray. Break equal-length ties by the smallest start. Return [-1,-1] if no such subarray exists or small is empty.
constraints: big contains 0..10000 signed 32-bit integers. small contains 0..100 distinct signed 32-bit integers; its entries are a set of required values, not a required sequence. Preserve both arrays and their order.
Repeated occurrences in big do not require extra matches. An empty target needs no nonempty window and uses [-1,-1] as its explicit representation. A missing target value yields [-1,-1] as well.
why: Expand the right edge until the window contains all required values, then shrink its left edge while that remains true. Track only required-value frequencies and how many required values are still absent. Unneeded values can be skipped at the left, and duplicate needed values can be removed until the last occurrence would disappear.
correctness: The frequency map always counts each required value inside the current window; missing equals the number with zero count. Thus missing=0 exactly characterizes a covering window. For each right edge, removing left entries until coverage would fail examines the shortest feasible window ending there. No discarded earlier left edge could give a shorter future window than the surviving one. Every right edge is processed, so the best recorded candidate is globally shortest. Strictly shorter updates during increasing right order preserve the earliest start among ties.
walkthrough: For big=[7,5,9,1,5,9,1] and small=[1,5,9], indices 1..3 contain 5,9,1 and cover the target in length three. Later windows 2..4 and 3..5 have the same length, so [1,3] remains the answer. Matching the target in its supplied order would incorrectly reject valid windows.
time: Expected O(big.length + small.length) time with hash-map operations; each window edge advances at most big.length times.
space: O(small.length) auxiliary map entries, plus the two-index output.
edges: Empty target, empty big array, missing target value.
Target values in a different order, redundant occurrences, and equal-length ties.
related: The public source describes a subarray covering a distinct required set, not an order-preserving subsequence problem.

description: The input contains all integers from 1 through n except two distinct missing values, in arbitrary order, with n=values.length+2. Return the two missing values in increasing order without modifying the input.
constraints: 2 <= n <= 100000. Input entries are distinct, lie in 1..n and omit exactly two values. No duplicates or out-of-range entries are admitted. For an empty input n=2 and the answer is [1,2].
Use O(1) auxiliary storage besides the two returned values. Do not sort or allocate a presence table proportional to n. Increasing result order is an explicit deterministic convention.
why: XOR the full range and the supplied entries: present values cancel, leaving a xor b for the missing pair. Because a and b differ, some bit is set in that XOR. Partition both the full range and input by one such bit; the two missing values land in different groups, and all present values cancel within their own groups.
correctness: Each present value appears twice in the full/input XOR and cancels, leaving exactly the two missing values. A set bit of their XOR means one missing value has that bit and the other does not. Repeating XOR separately for the two bit groups therefore leaves one missing value in each accumulator. These are the complete missing pair; ordering them changes no membership. All values and the selected low bit fit the admitted signed range, so no square sums or floating-point roots can overflow or round incorrectly.
walkthrough: For [1,3,5], n is 5 and the missing pair is 2,4. The combined XOR is 6 (binary 110); choosing its low set bit 2 separates 2 from 4. Present numbers cancel in each bit group, leaving those two values, returned as [2,4].
time: O(n) time for full-range and input XOR scans.
space: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage, excluding the two-value output.
edges: Empty input, missing endpoints, arbitrary input order.
The largest n; arithmetic square-sum formulas would exceed ordinary int bounds.
related: This is the two-missing follow-up established by the author source, not a one-missing-value substitution.
title: Missing Two

description: Process an integer stream in its given order and return the median immediately after each insertion. The median of an odd-sized prefix is its middle value in sorted order. For an even-sized prefix it is the arithmetic mean of the two middle values, using real arithmetic. Return one numeric value per input element; empty input returns [].
constraints: values is a nonnull array of 0..10000 signed 32-bit integers. Duplicates count as separate stream occurrences. Preserve the input array, order and every value.

Return actual medians, not doubled medians or truncated integers. Each admitted median is an integer or half-integer and is exactly representable as a double/Number/float. The result must match these values exactly. Compute even-prefix means without overflowing a signed 32-bit sum.
why: Keep the smaller half in a max heap and the larger half in a min heap. Their roots expose the two values surrounding the middle, so a median query needs no sorting. Balance sizes so the lower heap has either the same count or one extra occurrence; its root alone is then the odd median.
correctness: Insert each new value into the lower heap when it is no larger than its maximum, otherwise into the upper heap. This preserves that every lower value is at most every upper value. Moving a root between heaps restores size difference zero or one while preserving that order. For odd prefix length, the lower root has exactly half the other occurrences on either side and is the median. For even length, the lower maximum and upper minimum are the two central occurrences, so their widened average is the required median. Each insertion contributes one occurrence and each output observes the invariant after rebalancing.
walkthrough: For [5,1,9,2], the prefixes have sorted forms [5], [1,5], [1,5,9] and [1,2,5,9]. Medians are [5,3,5,3.5]. For [-2147483648,2147483647], the second median is -0.5; widening before summing prevents overflow.
time: O(n log(n+1)) total insertion time and O(1) median work per prefix.
space: O(n) heap storage plus O(n) returned medians; both heaps retain every inserted occurrence.
edges: Empty stream, single element and equal repeated values.
Increasing/decreasing streams, alternating extremes and negative half-integer medians.
Full signed endpoints and 10000 insertions.
related: The public stream API inserts a number and queries its current median. This batch wrapper performs those operations in order and returns every observed median, preserving streaming behavior without inventing unrelated scalar outputs.
title: Continuous Median

description: Return the total units of water trapped above a histogram after rainfall. Bars have width one, their nonnegative heights are given left to right, and water may escape past either end. Sum water above every position; do not return the area of one container formed by two chosen bars.
constraints: heights contains 0..10000 integers in 0..100000. The total volume is at most 1000000000 and fits signed 32-bit range. Preserve the array.
Empty input and fewer than three bars trap no water. Water above a bar is limited by the lower of the tallest barriers on its left and right, and cannot be negative.
why: Keep the tallest barrier seen from each end. The side with the lower established barrier can be settled now: the opposite barrier is already high enough to support that level. If the current bar raises its own barrier, it holds no water; otherwise its deficit is final. Move inward without allocating prefix/suffix arrays.
correctness: All positions outside the two pointers have been settled correctly. The two maxima record barriers already encountered on each side. If the left maximum is no greater than the right maximum, a left bar below that left maximum has exactly that water level: a left barrier establishes it, and the right barrier is high enough. A taller left bar raises the maximum and holds zero water. The symmetric argument settles a right position when the right maximum is smaller. Each step settles one position and preserves the invariant, so the accumulated deficits give the complete volume when the pointers cross.
walkthrough: For [3,0,2,0,4], the water above positions is [0,3,1,3,0], totaling 7. The interior height-2 bar reduces water at its own position by two units; using just the distance and end heights would overcount.
time: O(n) time: one pointer moves inward per iteration.
space: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage; no height-sized or input-sized arrays.
edges: Empty, short, monotone and all-zero histograms.
Several basins, equal end barriers, interior peaks, and maximum bounded volume.
related: Maximum two-line container area has a different objective and is not substituted for trapped histogram volume.
title: Volume of Histogram

description: Find a path of dictionary words from start to stop, changing exactly one letter at each step. Return both endpoints and every intermediate word, with no repeated word. Any valid such path is accepted; return [] when no transformation exists. If start==stop, return [start].
constraints: start and stop are nonempty lowercase ASCII words of the same length 1..8. dictionary contains 1..1000 nonempty lowercase ASCII words of length at most 8 and includes both endpoints. Duplicates are allowed and do not create new vertices; words of other lengths cannot participate.

Every returned word must be in dictionary, and each adjacent pair must differ in exactly one position. No letter insertion, deletion, transposition or arbitrary replacement of several letters is allowed. Preserve all inputs. The reference finds a shortest path, but shortest length is not a grading requirement.
why: Treat words as graph vertices and one-letter changes as edges. Breadth-first search discovers each word once and stores the predecessor that first reached it. Generate possible neighbors by changing one position to each other letter and checking dictionary membership, avoiding a comparison against every word for every step.
correctness: Every generated neighbor changes exactly one position and is queued only if it is a dictionary word, so every predecessor edge is a legal transformation. Visited tracking prevents repeated vertices and guarantees finite exploration. Induction on path length shows BFS discovers every reachable word; thus queue exhaustion proves no path exists. When stop is found, following predecessors back to start and reversing yields a valid path with both endpoints and no repeated word. The identical-endpoint case is the one-word path.
walkthrough: With dictionary=[cat,cot,cog,dog], start cat changes a to o to reach cot, then t to g to reach cog, then c to d to reach dog. Return [cat,cot,cog,dog]. cat->dog directly is invalid because several positions differ.
time: Expected O(D+26*W*L^2) character work for D dictionary characters, W reachable length-L words and copying/hashing each generated length-L candidate. At most 26*L candidates are tried per expanded word.
space: O(D+W*L) dictionary, visited/predecessor/queue and returned-word storage.
edges: Equal endpoints, disconnected components and direct one-letter neighbors.
Repeated dictionary entries, other word lengths, cycles and several valid paths.
related: The public variants differ on endpoints missing from the dictionary; this bank removes that uncertainty with an explicit endpoint-membership precondition and accepts every valid path.

description: Find the largest square submatrix whose entire border is black. Encode black as 0 and white as 1. Interior cells need not be black. Return [topRow,leftColumn,sideLength], using zero-based coordinates, or [] if no black cell exists. Among equal largest squares choose the smallest top row, then smallest left column.
constraints: matrix is nonnull and square with size 0..40 and entries only 0 or 1. An empty matrix has no square. A single black cell is a valid side-one square.
Preserve the outer array, every row object and every cell value. Check all four full edges, not just corners or the main diagonal. The result describes original coordinates.
why: Precompute how many consecutive black cells begin at each position going right and down. Four run-length checks then verify any candidate border in constant time. Search side lengths from largest to smallest and top-left positions in row order so the first valid candidate also satisfies the tie rule.
correctness: Processing cells from bottom-right computes exact right/down black-run lengths: a white cell has zero, while a black cell extends the adjacent run by one. A candidate of side s has an all-black border exactly when its top and bottom horizontal runs and left and right vertical runs each reach s. Interior values do not enter these checks. Descending sizes guarantee maximality of the first valid result; row/column order guarantees the requested earliest top-left tie. If no candidate succeeds, no side-one black cell exists either, so [] is correct.
walkthrough: For [[0,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,0]], all four length-three edges are black even though the center is white, so return [0,0,3]. Requiring a completely filled black square would incorrectly reject the correct answer.
time: O(n^3) time: O(n^2) preprocessing and O(n^3) candidates with four constant-time border checks.
space: O(n^2) auxiliary right/down run-length tables.
edges: Empty and all-white input; one black cell.
A hollow black border, a broken edge with black corners, and tied largest squares.
related: The source uses 0 for black. A maximum all-black filled square solves a different problem.
title: Max Black Square

description: Find a nonempty rectangular submatrix with greatest sum and return [sum,top,left,bottom,right], with all bounds zero-based and inclusive. For ties prefer smaller top, then smaller bottom, then smaller left, then smaller right. If either input dimension is empty, return [].
constraints: matrix is nonnull and rectangular, with 0..30 rows and 0..30 columns. Entries are integers in -1000000..1000000, so every rectangle sum fits signed 32-bit range. Preserve outer/row identities, dimensions and values.

For a nonempty matrix the selected rectangle must be nonempty, even if every entry is negative. Sum all cells in one rectangle; do not choose disconnected positive entries. Return coordinates as well as the sum.
why: Fix top and bottom rows and add their strip into one column-sum array. Any rectangle with those row bounds becomes a contiguous subarray of column sums. A nonempty Kadane scan finds the best such column interval in linear time. Extending the bottom row incrementally reuses column totals instead of resumming each rectangle.
correctness: For each row pair, each column total is exactly the sum between those rows. Therefore a column interval and its corresponding rectangle have identical sums. Kadane keeps the maximum nonempty sum ending at each column: extend a nonnegative preceding sum, or start anew after a negative one. Every possible rectangle has one enumerated row pair and column interval, so maximizing these candidates yields the global optimum. Keeping an equal-zero prefix favors earlier left bounds; strict global improvements with top/bottom iteration order preserve the specified tie priority. Initializing below all admitted sums prevents an empty zero choice from defeating all-negative rectangles.
walkthrough: For [[1,-2,3],[-4,5,6]], the bottom row interval columns 1..2 sums to 11. Including both rows over those columns gives -2+3+5+6=12, so return [12,0,1,1,2]. In [[-5,-2]], the correct nonempty answer is [-2,0,1,0,1], not zero.
time: O(rows^2*columns) time for all row pairs and their column scans.
space: O(columns) auxiliary column totals plus constant scalar bounds and the five-integer result.
edges: Empty dimensions, a single negative cell, all-negative matrices.
The entire matrix, a strict interior optimum, and ties under the stated top/bottom/left/right priority.
related: The result retains an actual maximizing rectangle, not only its sum; the tie order matches explicit row-pair then column-interval enumeration.
title: Max Submatrix

description: Return a rectangle of letters with the largest possible area such that every row, read left to right, and every column, read top to bottom, is a dictionary word. Return the rows as equal-length strings. Any maximum-area rectangle is accepted; return [] if no nonempty rectangle exists.
constraints: words is a nonnull array of 0..20 nonempty lowercase ASCII words, each 1..5 letters. Duplicate entries describe the same vocabulary word. The same word may be reused as multiple rows or columns; dictionary occurrences are not consumed.

A rectangle has positive height and width. Row words have length equal to width and column words length equal to height, so both dimensions are at most the largest dictionary word length. A square is not required. Preserve the input and all entries.
why: Try height/width pairs from largest area downward. For a fixed pair, append candidate row words and check whether every partial column is still a prefix of some dictionary word of the required column height. An impossible prefix can never be repaired by later rows, so pruning avoids exploring the rest of that branch.
correctness: Every completed accepted row sequence uses dictionary row words and has each full column in the required-height dictionary group, so it is a valid rectangle. At a partial state, a column prefix absent from every possible full column word cannot extend to any valid solution; rejecting it is safe. Trying every candidate row at each unpruned depth therefore finds a rectangle for those dimensions whenever one exists. Dimensions are considered in decreasing area, so the first successful rectangle has globally maximum area. Exhaustion proves no nonempty rectangle exists.
walkthrough: For words=[ab,ba], rows [ab,ba] make columns ab and ba, giving area 4. Rows [ba,ab] are another accepted maximum. With words=[aa], reusing aa twice gives [aa,aa], whose columns are also aa. With only [ab], no compatible column words exist, so return [].
time: Exponential search in the maximum word length L: O(D^L*(L+1)^4) conservative character work for at most D distinct dictionary words across O(L^2) dimension pairs, including copying/hashing column prefixes. L<=5 bounds this search; pruning can greatly reduce it.
space: O(D*(L+1)^2) dictionary/prefix characters plus O(L^2) candidate/result grid and O(L) recursion frames.
edges: Empty vocabulary, no compatible rectangle, one-letter words and nonsquare maxima.
Reused words, duplicate entries, equal-area alternate rectangles and column-prefix dead ends.
related: The public rectangle search permits repeated row choices and maximizes area. Returned rows replace its Rectangle wrapper while preserving both row/column word requirements.
title: Word Rectangle

description: Compute positive Jaccard similarities between distinct documents treated as sets of integer word IDs. Return one row [smallerDocumentId,largerDocumentId,intersectionSize,unionSize] for each pair with a nonempty intersection. The exact similarity is intersectionSize/unionSize; no floating-point rounding is involved. Sort result rows by the two document IDs.
constraints: documentIds has 0..200 distinct signed 32-bit IDs. documents has the same length; each nonnull row contains 0..200 distinct signed 32-bit word IDs. Document/word IDs are identities, not array positions or counts. Preserve both input arrays, every document row and all order/values.

Each returned pair appears once, with IDs in increasing order. Omit disjoint pairs, including pairs of empty documents. Counts are the actual intersection/union sizes, not reduced fraction components. Empty documents have no positive-similarity partner.
why: Most document pairs may share nothing. Build an inverted index from each word ID to the document positions containing it. A pair appears together once for each shared word, so incrementing only those pairs computes positive intersection sizes without testing every disjoint pair. Document lengths then give union=lengthA+lengthB-intersection.
correctness: Because each document contains a word ID at most once, a word posting list contributes exactly one increment to each pair sharing that word. Summing over words therefore yields the exact intersection count for every recorded pair, and records no zero-intersection pair. Inclusion-exclusion gives its exact union size. Mapping positions back to the supplied unique document IDs, normalizing pair orientation and sorting yields each required row once. Empty documents appear in no posting list and correctly contribute no positive pair.
walkthrough: For IDs [10,20,30] and documents [[1,2],[2,3],[]], word 2 links documents 10 and 20 once. Their intersection is 1 and union is 2+2-1=3, so return [[10,20,1,3]], representing exact similarity 1/3. Empty document 30 creates no positive pair.
time: Expected O(T+sum(f_w^2)+P log(P+1)) time for T word occurrences, posting frequency f_w per word and P positive document pairs. Posting-pair work can still be quadratic when many documents share words.
space: O(T+P+n) inverted postings, sparse intersection counters and result rows for n documents; no dense n-by-n matrix is allocated.
edges: No documents, empty/disjoint documents and identical sets.
Arbitrary/signed-endpoint document IDs, input order differing from ID order and several shared words.
Word duplicates inside one document are outside the set-input domain.
related: Exact intersection/union counts represent the public task's Jaccard value without decimal tolerance ambiguity. Original document IDs are retained rather than silently replacing them with positions.

languageWhy.csharp: C# Dictionary counters use the sparse key i*n+j for document positions i<j. This is a unique address below n*n, not a dense matrix allocation. Output maps through documentIds and uses CompareTo for ordering, avoiding overflow from subtracting arbitrary signed IDs.
languageWhy.java: Java HashMap stores only positive pair counters, keyed by i*n+j. Posting lists are built in increasing document position order, so each shared-word pair has one orientation. Integer.compare orders original signed IDs safely after decoding the position key.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ unordered_map stores only observed posting pairs. Position keys stay below 40000, and union counts stay below 401, so the signed arithmetic/casts are safe. The final vector is sorted lexicographically after positions are mapped to the supplied IDs.
languageWhy.python: Python divmod decodes each sparse i*n+j counter back to document positions. The actual IDs may be negative or in a different order, so the returned pair is normalized separately. Dictionary counters count shared words; no decimal division or fraction reduction changes those counts.
languageWhy.javascript: JavaScript Map keys encode document positions below 40000, exactly representable as Numbers. Original signed IDs are normalized only when constructing output rows; their numeric sort differences also remain exact. Counts are integer intersection/union sizes, not rounded ratios.
